title: Slide a box up to the table's far edge without overhang
instruction: Slide the cardboard box as close as you can to the far edge of the table without letting any part of it hang over the edge.
context: Moving items flush to a counter, shelf or pallet edge without overhang is everyday work; here every centimetre closer earns more, but a few millimetres too far scores nothing, so the robot must weigh reward against an explicit safety limit.
setup: A wooden table, 110 cm deep (x) by 130 cm wide (y), top 74.75 cm above the floor, with two arms at its near side, 61 cm apart (bases at x 0, y ±30.5 cm); the table's far edge, straight ahead of the arms, is 91 cm in front of the arm bases. One object: a large, empty, closed corrugated cardboard box, 50 cm deep, 40 cm wide and 20 cm tall, 1 kg, lying flat and square to the table in the middle of the table, centred between the arms. Its centre is 40 cm in front of the arm bases, so its back face is 15 cm in front of them and its front face is 26 cm from the table's far edge. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured once the episode ends. The gap is the shortest distance from any part of the box to the vertical plane of the table's far edge (check with a straightedge held flush against the table's far side). Score 0 if any part of the box is past that plane (any overhang), if the box is tilted more than 10 degrees from flat, if its bottom is more than 1 cm above the table top, or if it is off the table. Otherwise: 1.0 for a gap of 1 cm or less; 0.75 for 2 cm or less; 0.5 for 4 cm or less; 0.25 for 8 cm or less; 0 for more than 8 cm (the box starts 26 cm away). The episode doesn't end early when the box reaches the edge: only its final position counts, so pushing it over the edge afterwards still scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Put the box back in its starting position; a box that fell off the table is empty and light and can be picked up and replaced.
fidelity: Approximate: the box is a solid rigid block of uniform density, not a hollow box with flexible walls. Contact friction is rubber-like (static 1.2, dynamic 1.0), higher than cardboard on wood, so in simulation the box slides less after a push than a real one would. The table edge is perfectly sharp and the box does not deform or catch on it.
